Question eight. How does a support vector machine, an SVM, work? It finds the boundary with the widest margin between the classes. The points on or inside the margin are the support vectors, and they alone fix it. The kernel trick bends that boundary without building new features. On two noisy rings, a straight boundary scores fifty-four percent; a radial basis function kernel, eighty-nine. The follow-up is cost. Where classes overlap, many rows become support vectors, here five thousand three hundred of twenty thousand, and every prediction checks them all. Doubling the rows more than tripled the fit time, measured once in the browser's Python. Distances, margins and gradients all take a feature's units at face value.

Question nine. What is feature scaling, and why does it matter? It puts features on comparable ranges, by standardizing or min-max scaling. Simulate customers whose age, in years, and income, in dollars, matter equally. Unscaled, kNN scores seventy-four and a half percent, exactly what income alone scores: in raw distance, the whole span of ages counts for no more than fifty dollars. Standardized, eighty-nine. Multiply one of the page's columns by a hundred, as if dollars became cents, and gradient descent goes from eight steps to nearly eighty thousand. Distance models, regularized models and gradient training need it; trees don't. And fit the scaler on training data only, then ship it with the model.
